en: Having bowed to that stainless [Lord], a concise commentary is composed for the sake of understanding the words in this supreme treatise, the *Śivārkamaṇidīpikā*, specifically regarding the section known as the *Vidyāpāda*;

for the determination of the meaning of the categories (*padārtha*) has already been explained by me at length elsewhere through reasoning and scripture, being common [to all systems] and intended primarily to cut away doubts concerning the established conclusion (*kṛtānta*).
Having seen Hara seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, Tārkṣya spoke these words preceded by praise: KirT_1.1 //
Victory to you, expert in severing the bonds of the broad-shouldered Andhaka;
victory to you, the preeminent lord of heroes who burnt down the cities besieged by him!
Victory to you, O Terrifier who severed the heads of all the lords of the gods!
Victory to you, whose power is renowned, the destroyer of the stability of Manmatha!
Victory to you, who destroyed the body of Acyuta and removed the power of the Kālakūṭa poison;
victory to you, who restrained the force of the river’s current during its great, swirling turbulence!
Victory to you, who deluded the wives of the sages in the Dārūvana grove;
victory to you, who were formidable in the violent agitation caused by the great onset of your dance-play.
Victory to you, who terrify the gods and asuras with the fury of your fierce form!
Victory to you, who have displayed magnificent torrents of blood from the mouths of cruel lords of men!
Victory to you, O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice through the prowess of heroic exertion!
Victory to you, who are proud of the strength inherent in the manifestation of the wondrous Great Liṅga!
Victory to you, O fierce one with white omens, who causes the falling away of the body of death!
Victory to you, O Daughter of the Mountain, who are the abode of all happiness and are unassailable by desire and delusion! KirT_1.8 //
Victory to you, O dispeller of the darkness of the net of delusion and the fever of suffering!
Victory to you, the burner of the worlds above and below, from the netherworld to the peak of existence!
O Śiva, tell me, who am your devotee and full of fear,
the supreme knowledge by attaining which all men reach absolute liberation.
Thus addressed, Hara, whose crest-jewel is the shimmering moon, spoke.
The Blessed One said:
"This which you have asked is auspicious; listen to this knowledge of great exaltation. (KirT 1.11)
The great tantra named *Kiraṇa* bestows the bliss of supreme nectar;
it is all-encompassing, pure, clearly illuminating the nature of reality, and manifest.
It sets forth the investigation of the knowledge concerning the Lord, the fettered souls, and the fetters;
it is endowed with ritual action and conduct, and brings about the weight of yogic power.
Garuḍa said: "If that is so, then what kind of beast is it that is bound, and how? How is it liberated? Tell me this for the sake of dispelling my doubt. (KirT 1.14)
The Blessed One said:

"The individual soul (paśu) is eternal, indeed formless, ignorant, inactive, devoid of qualities, and powerless; it is all-pervading, situated within the belly of Māyā, and does not deliberate upon the means for its own enjoyment. (KirT 1.15)
From Śiva, *kalā* comes into connection with that impure [soul];
by it, consciousness is empowered, and its sphere of experience is made manifest by *vidyā*.
Colored by passion and yet being the primary principle through its nature of the qualities (guṇas),
the bound soul (paśu) is fettered due to its connection with the array of instruments beginning with the intellect (buddhi).

Then, due to the influence of destiny (*niyati*), one is constrained even regarding what has been earned by oneself; deluded by the experience of the effects of time and its enumeration, one is bound by time.
Thus, bound by the principles (tattva) and the constituent parts (kalā), possessing limited knowledge and joined with a body,
embraced by the enjoyment of Māyā, identified with that [world], he is veiled by the innate nature (sahaja).
Then, when his karma has become balanced due to the force of time, he enjoys the entirety of his experience, such as pleasure and so forth, according to his own past actions. (KirT 1.20)
When one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of intense power,
he becomes omniscient like Śiva himself, being entirely devoid of limited knowledge.
At that time, the transmigrating being is no longer [merely] a wanderer, but is fully perfected in the manifestation of Śiva-nature;
thus, being gradually bound, one is liberated through the yoga of gradual progression.
The Puruṣa is traditionally taught to exist in three states: as the Kevala (isolated), the Sakala (with kalās), and the Śuddha (pure).
Such a being is declared to be a Paśu (bound soul); what else do you wish to ask?
Garuḍa said:
"Regarding that Self which has been described by you as both the knower of a little and the all-knowing Śiva—
tell me the cause for these two, whose natures are respectively pure and impure."
The Blessed One said:
"Because of his connection with beginningless impurity, he is described by me as the one who knows only a little;
because of his liberation from beginningless impurity, he is the omniscient Śiva."
When the state of having a beginning is established, then a cause is postulated;
by those two, it is remembered as being of such a nature—pure or impure according to reality.
Why is crystal pure, and why is copper stained with impurities?
For just as there is no such cause in this case, so too there is none for Śiva and the self.
Garuḍa said:
"For what reason, O Lord, is the Self bound by the bond of the *kalās* and so forth? And why is it said by you that, while being all-pervasive, it is nonetheless contained within *māyā*?"
Since it is all-pervasive, how could it reside everywhere within the belly of illusion?
Because they are mutually contradictory, how can this be possible?
The Blessed One said:
"That animal is bound for the sake of liberation; otherwise, that [liberation] does not arise for it. As long as attachment to the body has not ceased, it does not enjoy its experience."
This body of his is an illusion; because that [true nature] is absent, there is no liberation.
Due to being rendered impure by this or that [defilement], he is made turbid through his lack of self-sovereignty.
Just as a cloth, though containing impurities within due to its inherent defects, becomes purified,
so too does an impure person, even while remaining within the womb of Māyā.
For that which is called Māyodara is characterized by the earth element at the end of the sequence beginning with Kalā;
and the dissolution into it that has been taught is intended with reference to the subtle body.

Garuḍa said: You have described impurity as beginningless and consisting of Māyā; tell me, is that impurity identical with this Self, or is it distinct from its qualities? Of what nature is impurity? KirT 2.11.
The Blessed One said:
"Defilement is innate (sahaja), while the effect of *māyā* is adventitious (*āgāmika*) defilement.
*Māyā* is said not to be delusive; by its very nature, it is illuminating through its effects. (KirT 2.12)
For, by means of its own activity which is conjoined with it and which illuminates consciousness,
this [power] tears apart the impurity and brings about the manifestation of consciousness in a single part.
She abides as the illuminator and does not abide in the state of deluding effects;
illumination is expressed by the word "manifestation" (vyakti), and obscuration by the word "impurity" (mala).
The manifestation of the path is clearly said to be free from impurity, like a lamp dispelling darkness;
likewise, Māyā is said to be delusive due to the enjoyment of tasting sense objects. (KirT 2.15)
Wherever this [individual] may abide, due to the cause of the impurity of his own karma,
bondage arising from illusion proceeds for him along with its objective basis.
"Would it not follow that even Śiva, though freed from beginningless impurity, would [still be bound]?
Therefore, by logical reasoning, Māyā is certainly not distinct from Mala. (KirT 2.17)
The entire effect of illusion would [then] exist; whence could there be any other innate impurity?
That state of being a bound soul (paśutva) would reside within the Self, and even the bound soul would be situated in the midst of the paths.
That by which [the self] is considered bound is declared to be impurity (mala), which has a characteristic distinct from that [self].
Impurity is ignorance, the state of being a fettered soul (paśutva), and the obscuring darkness (tamas). (KirT 2.19)
For ignorance (avidyā), obscuration (āvṛti), and stupor (mūrchā) are stated to be its synonyms;
and it is established in various philosophical systems through the distinctions of such synonyms as ignorance and the rest. (KirT 2.20)
Because of its existence, the bound soul (paśu) is considered here to be that which is to be bound, purified, and awakened;
those functions such as being bound and so forth are proclaimed to be its various states.
"When he exists as a male, these [powers] arise, and not merely the state of being an enjoyer.
Garuḍa said:
"If it is thus established that his impurity (mala), which binds him like a noose, is associated with the bound soul (paśu)..."
"Why is this impurity not logically conceived as a property (dharma) of the self?
The Blessed One replied:
"Because of its beginningless connection with the self, it is metaphorically designated as a property. (KirT 2.23)
How could that which is endowed with knowledge come to possess the quality of ignorance?
Its nature would not clearly undergo a transformation into something other than its own true nature. (KirT 2.24)
If the quality of consciousness were subject to transformation in the person (puruṣa), then while knowledge would be manifest in one [person], it would be concealed in another. (KirT 2.25)
The transformation of that which is insentient is not possible for that which is sentient.
Garuḍa said:
"And because of their beginningless connection, there can be no separation between them due to their all-pervasiveness."
"When the innate [impurity] has reached its exhaustion, would there not be its destruction?
The Blessed One replied:
"Even for this pervasive impurity, the destruction of its power is brought about. (KirT 2.27)
By means of skillful methods, the power residing in impurity is somehow restrained;
just as the burning power of fire is quickly suppressed by a mantra. (KirT 2.28)
In the same way, due to the suppression of that power, it is said to be "disjoined";
having suppressed that power, one becomes free from longing for worldly existence.
The innate [impurity] is simultaneous with the copper, yet its destruction does not entail the destruction of that [copper];
just as there is a destruction of the copper, so too is there a destruction of the impurity of the person.
Just as when the husk of rice is removed, its [inherent] essence is not destroyed, and just as the potency associated with poison is neutralized by mantras; KirT 2.31.
Just as that poison is not destroyed [by the fruit], so too is the destruction of a person's impurity;
it is like the fruit of the *kataka* tree cast into turbid water.
Just as one who restrains his vital energy (śakti) does not discharge it elsewhere than into water, so too does the knowledge of Śiva effect the restraint of that [energy]. 2.33.
Garuḍa said:
The state of being an enjoyer is said to arise from impurity; would it not also arise from desire?
Since that [desire] arises from passion, why should passion here be described as arising from impurity? (KirT 3.1)
The Blessed One said:
That which is called "the state of being an enjoyer" has its cause in beginningless impurity; when that body exists, for what reason does desire arise toward it? (KirT 3.2)
Passion also arises in a person because it has that [desire] as its cause;
for just as the binding of shackles depends upon the seed of theft.
Thus, having regard for the state of being a bound soul (paśu), the principle of attachment (rāgatattva) proceeds;
from this arises its status as an enjoyer, while the body and the objects of enjoyment arise from other causes.
For the state of being an enjoyer exists through the condition of being a bound soul (paśu); the bondage of Māyā resides within the body.
The experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth for the bound soul is established through karma;
otherwise, this bondage consisting of the state of being an enjoyer and the act of enjoyment would not have been described.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord of Gods, this action which has been described as the cause of experience occurs when the body exists;
but at the time of creation, from where does the body come?"
The Blessed One said:
Just as that impurity is beginningless, so too is karma beginningless.
If this variety were not established as beginningless, by what cause would it arise? (KirT 3.7)
Therefore, karma is beginningless, and likewise is illusion and existence;
similarly, Śiva stands as the beginningless creator of the entire universe.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, you have declared Śiva to be the creator; how can he be reached?
Since he is formless due to his being beyond the elements, how is his status as a creator logical?"
The Blessed One said: "Just as time, though formless, is seen to bring about results, so too Śiva, though formless, accomplishes his work through his will. (KirT 3.10)
Intention alone is its instrument, as is held by those who possess immediate yoga;
for a fisherman is seen to extract a thorn even when devoid of [physical] organs.
No external activity is observed, yet the effect is understood to arise from intention.
The gross and variegated effect cannot exist otherwise than through a cause, just like a jar; therefore, there must be some cause, for action is not insentient.
He is declared to be the partless (niṣkala), the gross (sthūla), and likewise the part-and-whole (sakalaniṣkala);
as Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta, he is differentiated according to the distinction of his functions.
Garuḍa said:
How can he who is partless (niṣkala) be known as having parts (sakala) at that time?
For one who possesses two natures is another [kind of being] entirely contradictory to himself. (KirT 3.14)
The Blessed One said:

"By the descent of the power [of the teacher] upon the disciple, and always by the power of the mantra, the partless [reality] is perceived through that power, like a subtle change in poison. (KirT 3.15)
Even though a person is complete, he is not [identical to Śiva] because he lacks the components of Māyā;
since Śiva is pure, no dark *kalās* (limited powers) are to be postulated here for him.
The constituent parts (kalās) of that [deity] consist of mantra, and those mantras are essentially Śiva;
by means of them, one should fashion for oneself a great body presided over by the pure syllables.
As long as one does not act in this way, the lineage of the Guru does not bestow grace upon any embodied beings whatsoever. (KirT 3.18)
Just as a yogin possesses power both in seizing and in releasing,
so too should one understand here the seizing and releasing of the All-pervading Lord.
Through the mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras, and through the threefold activities of accomplishment,
everything is perceived through meditation by means of the engagement of all-encompassing gnosis.
Another deity who is said to belong to two natures is not partless;
with respect to his vast body, he is traditionally known as "devoid of parts" (kalāhīna).
Thus the Lord himself abides as the cause of yoga for yogins;
yet yoga is not [found] in the channels nor in retention, because it lacks a defining characteristic.
For the sake of favoring men, the Supreme has assumed the state of the non-Supreme,
reaching as far as sound (nāda), the point (bindu), space (kha), mantra, the atom (anu), power (śakti), the seed-syllable (bīja), and the digit (kalā).
The yogi, being grateful for the assistance received, bestows the fruit because of his omniscience;
through his power to grant grace according to one's wishes, he possesses the authority over dissolution, enjoyment, and the office [of governance].
He is shown to be threefold according to the distinction of his functions and by the distinction of his names;
this Īśvara impels the lords of the sciences who reside below.
Merely impelled by him, they create the lower world;
Śiva is declared the agent in the pure path, while Ananta is the lord in the impure.
Just as one appointed by the Lord of the Earth acts as his equal sovereign,
so does he perform everything, awakened by that power;
he is omniscient, possesses a pure body, and is the illuminator of all knowledge.
Garuḍa said:
"Indeed, it is through the power of Śiva’s Śakti that Ananta awakens;
and that awakening Śakti is proclaimed to be omnipresent."
Why does it not produce cognition even in others who are proximate?
If [you argue] that it assists only those who are fit, then Śiva would be possessed of passion. (KirT 4.2)
The Blessed One said:
"Is it not the case that, through contact with the rays of the sun, the awakening of lotuses is uniform?
Yet some awaken while others never do at all."
Attachment and aversion do not exist in the sun, nor do they exist in the Lord;
for His activity proceeds from His office, and there is no maintenance of that office without activity.
"O Bird, by virtue of that [power], Ananta would possess omniscience.
Garuḍa said: "Omniscience is not possible for Ananta as long as he possesses a physical body. KirT 4.5.
Since the sense faculties are fixed and their respective objects of apprehension are also fixed,
that body— which is illusory in nature— is born from the cause of residual karma.
"If there were indeed a distinction, such as the ability to hear from a great distance and so forth," the Blessed One said,
"his body is said to consist of pure *yoni* and is not born of karma."
Since he is thus liberated from the bonds, by what could his knowledge be obstructed?
Just as the venom of a snake residing within it does not afflict that [person] once he has left it, so too [knowledge] does not cause harm when it has departed from him.
In this way, the accumulation of fetters residing therein does not afflict the infinite one;
just as a severed sprout might arise again by virtue of its dependence on a location, so it would be here.
Through the yoga of abiding in the Lord of Mantras, the body is maintained by force;
by the power of the mantra, the body remains sustained for a long time. (KirT 4.10)
Even one bitten by the serpent of Time attains his desired state through the power [of the mantra];
for it is by the efficacy of that power that his body remains as it is.
Therefore, the body should be known as utterly pure, like a lotus leaf;
it is rendered fit by the tantras, just as the vital essence within the body is refined.
In the same way, that immensely powerful awakening abides within this body;
it is like the supreme strength that arises from the potency of medicine for those who are otherwise powerless.
By the power and efficacy of that [consciousness], it enters the supreme strength of the Infinite;
through that application of power, it impels the womb in an instant.
Garuḍa said:
"What is the use of a prompter for Māyā in its lower path,
since it is subject to transformation in this world by its own inherent modification?"

Since the world is declared to have its source therein, and the *kalās* and other principles are its modifications (*vikāra*), the destruction of everything would follow from modification; how then could the world not be a modification? (KirT 4.16)
The Blessed One said:
Because it is insentient, that [prakṛti] is to be impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa;
since there is no modification [of prakṛti] from itself, its impeller is therefore infinite.
Just as the ocean, due to the force of the wind, undergoes transformation only on its surface,
so too Māyā, because of its unshakeable nature, possesses transformations through the categories beginning with *kalā*.
If she were not agitated, she would not perform an action; if there were agitation of her, that would be her movement.
Thus, that power, being impelled by him, would constantly produce effects. (KirT 4.19)
Akṣobhyā has been described as being established as the cause of the world due to her omnipresence (*vibhutva*).

Just as Māyā is predominant by pervading [the path], so too the group of her effects does not [pervade] the path; rather, Akṣobhyā is traditionally remembered as being established by pervading the entities beginning with *kalā*. (KirT 4.20)
The power that effects its own result is called action; though subtle in form, it resides within gross effects, just as [the potentiality] exists within the seed of a banyan tree.
Therefore, that [kalā] should be known as the cause of this gross [universe] on all sides;
hence kalā is established as *tuṭi*, for it is indeed the awakener and the creator of desire. (KirT 4.22)

Subtler than these [gross elements] are the qualities; from them arises intellect (*buddhi*), and from intellect, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*). From that [ego-sense] arise the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); from those, the gross elements are born. The Lord creates all this below.
Thus the Lord Īśa, endowed with Śiva-śakti,
created the entire effect consisting of Māyā, which is a mixture of the pure and the impure.
If it were born from a womb, it would arise from a difference in cognition; if that [cognition] were one, how could it be twofold?
Furthermore, such a thing is seen in fireflies and the like, which are produced by diverse causes and thus contradict the claim of a single cause.

Thus, that effect, which arises from the causal power and is born from the seed as its instrumental cause, should be known as having a distinct configuration, composed of both pure and impure limbs. In this way,
that effect, which is the basis for the physical body, has been fully explained.
Although these effects are mutually contradictory and of a non-black nature,
nevertheless, they are clearly and perfectly integrated within a single object.
One should accomplish the distinct purpose of man, as in the case of the parts of a man's chariot;
in this same way, this bond of the body was created by the Infinite One.
There is no liberation without the body, nor is there enjoyment, for the Guru is the master of consciousness and action.
And Śambhu, the peaceful one who bestows grace upon all, effects this by virtue of his autonomy and sovereignty; through his power, the entire fruit [of existence] arises.
Garuḍa said:

Initiation occurs through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); the descent does not result from [Śiva’s] omnipresence (*vibhutva*), for because Śiva is omnipresent, he is always already present within the bound soul (*paśu*).
Since power is always present, why would there not be the cessation of worldly existence?
Or if it is time [that causes this], what is that "time" said to be? If it is Śiva, then what need is there for time? (KirT 5.2)
The Blessed One said:
"In this world, the application of words is seen to occur through figurative usage;
for example, although the omnipresent Self is eternal and a goer, it is also spoken of as perishable."
Just as the severing of the fetters was described as the Lord Śiva, the King of Mantras,
so too is the descent of power (śaktinipāta) described by way of metaphorical usage.
Just as the sudden fall of an object causes fear,
so too is the descent of power said to bestow the fear of worldly existence.
Therefore, the self likewise moves toward another teacher;
just as a guru might wake sleeping disciples from behind with a staff.
Śiva, too, awakens those sleeping in the slumber of delusion by means of his power;
when the realization of one's true nature has occurred, it is then said that [the soul] has fallen [into grace].
Therefore, there would be a discharge of potency, and that discharge signifies a sign;
the time of that discharge is the very equality of the karmas.
Whether the duration of the action is equal, exhausted, or unequal—how can that equality be known, and how can there be a difference of even a single *tuṭi*?
Such subtle equality exists at the very moment [the action occurs]. (KirT 5.9)
Indeed, by the power of the mark of awakening, it quickly illuminates its own nature;
that which was previously the predominant portion of karma is the giver of experience, while the other is otherwise.
If there were equality [of merit and demerit], how could experience arise for anyone? Or if the initiating karma were mixed, then there would be no experience when [the two] are equal. (KirT 5.11)
And some further [distinction] must be stated; otherwise, there would be no "other than pleasure.
Because of the relationship between the greater and the lesser, confusion does not arise. (KirT 5.12)
Because it is deficient, excessive, or empty, one goes to that state;
that should be understood as a downfall, for his devotion is of a different character. (KirT 5.13)
Time alone is that which is proficient in the appropriation of power by the Self;
Śiva, due to the connection with beginningless karma, depends upon time.
The Knower of Reality, the Blessed Śiva, has declared this to be the "gap of time" (kālacchidra);
it is like someone who, when at a moving target, waits for a certain moment. (Kirātārjunīya 5.15)
Even though he is the Knower, Śiva likewise awaits that same time;
otherwise, because of the absence of equality with them, there would be simultaneous liberation for all.

If that sequence is not accepted because it does not depend on the means of accomplishment (*upāya-sādhana*), then Śiva is to be known as the Lord (*prabhu*) in this matter; for what is considered to be the nature of lordship other than [the power of] *tuṭi*? 5.17.
Sovereignty exists because of the nature of consciousness; however, one who is ignorant is not a sovereign.
Sovereignty occurs when time is present, just as the sun possesses sovereignty [over its light] upon the awakening of the lotus.
And yet, without time, no blossoming occurs there;
nevertheless, in this world, the sun is proclaimed to be the awakener of the lotus.
If that fitness is also [determined by] time, then time too is metaphorically a signifier.
Thus, although there is equality between the action and time itself,
nevertheless, the Lord Īśa remains the master here over the descent of power (śaktipāta).
If one asks how that single [consciousness], being one, can produce cognition for many, there is no fault even in this case; because of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*), it is not obstructed.
Thus has the subtle conjunction of powers been explained here in this teaching.
Garuḍa said:
"If initiation is established in this way through that conjunction of powers..."
Even after the time of initiation, concealment is observed;
if the power that effects concealment remains in him, there is no liberation.
"May that Lord act in such a way that he does not become otherwise. The Blessed One said:
"By the will of Śiva, she [the power] belongs to those men who have attained invisibility. (KirT 5.24)
She is not called "the Concealer" (tirohikā) because she performs concealment;
for she does not cause a fall into concealment, since her nature is one of grace.
At the very moment when [the time] is most imminent, she reveals herself;
having revealed herself, that power which awakens the person departs like a flash of lightning. (KirT 5.26)
If this [individual], even though initiated, were concealed in his entirety, then in both types of concealment, the attainment of a [divine] station would occur somewhere. (KirT 5.27)
For one who remains therein, that very same latent impression (vāsanā) arises;
for one endowed with that, there occurs the non-conceptual liberation of the self.
By this sequential yoga, one may attain disappearance;
for if liberation were not that [disappearance], there would be the consequence of its being purposeless. (KirT 5.29)
The power [of the mind] becomes dull and even more dull due to the intended equivalence of karma;
however, that power does not undergo transformation like milk.
For the power of the possessor of power resides in the differentiation of functions and forms;
that ladder of castes, beginning with the twice-born, clearly brings about liberation.
Garuḍa said:
Śiva, the supreme cause, is declared to be the benefactor of all;
yet there are those twice-born castes who exist in states of relative superiority or inferiority.

If the formative impression (*saṃskāra*) were also to be thus [momentary], why would the fruit not likewise be so? How could there be a variation in degree—whether inferior or superior—for those impressions that are identical? (KirT 6.2)
The Blessed One said:
"The purification of a living being is not considered to belong to its birth nor to its body;
for if it belonged to birth, then when one person is initiated, everyone would be initiated."
Therefore, it is not said that [the body] possesses birth, for it is considered insentient;
rather, Śiva is declared to be the benefactor of all, bestowing grace upon the nature of consciousness.
Garuḍa said:
O Lord, because you are the bestower of grace upon all—including children, the ignorant, and even serpents—you must extend that grace;
and that grace must be preceded by ritual consecration (saṃskāra).
When it is stated in the Tantra that liberation occurs through ritual action alone, then practices such as ritual performance, knowledge, and vows are not the means [to liberation]. (KirT 6.6)
The Blessed One said:
"O Tārkṣya, the Lord bestows grace exactly according to how beings are situated.
Some among them are fit for ritual action, and their liberation is likewise accordingly."
Likewise, some are fit for knowledge, while others are fit for conduct;
thus, for those to whom liberation has been proclaimed, it occurs through union with the Lord.
Initiation is held to be the cause of the means, such as knowledge and the rest;
liberation does not occur through initiation alone, for it is that [initiation] which serves as the regulator of the means.
Because they bring about the benefit of all beings, they are proclaimed as "means" (upāya).
Why is it that [the Buddha] did not proclaim a single means, but rather taught otherwise? KirT_6.10 //
One should purify the commitments (samaya) regarding women and so forth due to one's own incapacity;
there is no fault if it is done out of ignorance, but if done knowingly, the fault becomes great. (KirT 6.11)
By that, their liberation shall come through initiation and the yoga of devotion;
however, for those who are capable in this regard, there is nothing to be purified—this one should reveal to them.
In this way, he should reveal all things, such as knowledge and so forth, to one who is capable;
otherwise, there would be a collapse of stability, yet stability is taught in the Śiva-āgama. (KirT 6.13)
In its absence, nothing would exist; therefore, this rule is established with the intention of explaining the means for its persistence through its quality of being the benefactor of all.
Garuḍa said:
"It is said that initiation (dīkṣā) is indeed performed for the purpose of severing the bonds;
yet, even that severance is not perceived. Tell me, how can this be so?"
The Blessed One said:
"The destruction [of obstacles] through the paralyzing of the noose has been accomplished even by the perfected Śambaras;
for the Śambaras are inconceivable, just as [the power of] physical poison is neutralized."
Just as someone is brought under control merely by the recitation of their name from afar by means of the most eminent mantras, so too here is the destruction of karma.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, if the severance of all fetters occurs through initiation once the goal has been accomplished,
how can there be the continued existence of the body?"
The Blessed One said:
Just as the wheel continues to spin even after the completion of the jar has occurred, being sustained by prior momentum, so too does this body persist. (KirT 6.19)

Karma that would otherwise lead to many future existences is, like a burnt seed, obstructed by subtle [defilements]; for it is through the experience [of its results] that this [karma] is brought to an end.
Upon the fall of the body, there shall be liberation, or it may grant immediate nirvāṇa;
because they are always perfected by means of the subtle bodies of their effects, they are the ones who unite one with Śiva.
Garuḍa said:
Why is not even the slightest mark of one liberated from the noose seen here through the mark of devotion? Nor is any mark clearly visible anywhere.
Even where [the reason] is clearly observed [to be present], there too it is subject to deviation;
its application, as previously stated, must be preceded by the apprehension of that [reason] through logical reasoning.
Because of its all-pervasiveness, there is no grasping of it, and likewise because of its formlessness;
there would be a great contradiction here—explain this to me.
The Blessed One said: "The sign of that [attainment] is the culmination of latent impressions (vāsanā) and non-conceptuality regarding those actions.
For how could this, which resides within the body, be inferred even by means of vibration? (KirT 6.25)
Just as space is pervasive, and just as the formless poison is apprehended through the power of a mantra, so too is that quality, which possesses such power, to be expressed.
O Bird, the atoms of mantra are to be known through the union of the signified and the signifier. (KirT 6.26)
